lessons.title: Spot versus a story
lessons.content:
# Spot versus a story

A candlestick is a picture of matches that already happened. **Spot** is not that picture. Spot is inventory: units you hold now, or a company row that claims you hold them. The next match has not occurred. A story about the next match is not a position.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to split one ticker into three objects — self-custody spot, a centralised-exchange IOU, and a perpetual — and refuse to treat a sentence that names Crystal Stones as a long from this school.

## Three objects, one ticker

The same letters can name three different machines.

**Self-custody spot.** A mapping in a token contract (or a native balance) that lists your address. Transfer is a signed transaction. The explorer can show the row. Loss modes: you sign a hostile transaction, you leak a seed, the contract is hostile, you send to the wrong chain.

**Centralised-exchange spot.** A database row at a company. The company (or its custodians) holds keys. Your screen is not an explorer. Withdrawal is a request. Loss modes: insolvency, freeze, outage, wrong-network credit, a password or API key that walks out the door.

**Perpetual.** A derivative that tracks an index. You do not hold the coin. You hold a contract with a mark, a margin, and a kill switch. You cannot withdraw the underlying. You can close if the engine still accepts the close. Loss modes: liquidation, funding bleed, venue death, mark games.

Naming the ticker does not name the object. “I am in CST” is three possible sentences.

## What a candle is not

A candle records open, high, low, close of matches on **that venue’s** book or curve for **that interval**. It does not record the other venue. It does not record your fill. It does not record fees. It does not promise the next interval.

Treating a green candle as a reason is how inventory becomes a mood. This course maps venues. It does not narrate candles into homework.

## Crystal Stones is not a long

Crystal Stones may appear as a ticker on a book, a pair, or a sentence. This academy’s relationship to that contract is **verify-only**: `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BNB Smart Chain, **chain ID 56**. Reading a contract is not opening a position. A Mentor message that names a target on that ticker is a **malfunction**. Report it. Do not treat it as a desk.

TABLE
Object | What you hold | What you can withdraw | Kill switch
Self-custody spot | Token mapping or native units | The asset, if you can sign and the contract allows | None from a venue engine
CEX spot IOU | A company ledger row | Whatever the company still sends | Freeze, queue, insolvency
Perpetual | A derivative on an index | Cash residual if the venue pays it | Liquidation on the venue’s mark
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
TICKER LETTERS
  |-- self-custody row (chain)
  |-- company IOU (ledger)
  +-- perpetual (engine)
ENDDIAGRAM

## Rails for this course (once)

Intermediate tuition is **$10 USDT BEP-20 on academy checkout**. Not Crystal Stones. Not a chat address. Not a “pay in CST to unlock signals.” Gas on BSC is **BNB**. Staff never ask for a seed, a key, 2FA codes, or remote control. This course will not tell you to open a trade.

## What this academy refuses on day one

No entries. No leverage invites. No “easy 2%.” No weekly calls. The signal box is empty because there is no desk. If you insist on touching a venue anyway, the only honest size is money whose disappearance does not require a story. That is not homework. The homework is naming the object.

NOTE
Tuition is $10 USDT BEP-20 on the academy checkout page. Crystal Stones at 0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00 on chain 56 is a contract to verify, not a pair this school assigns. Gas is BNB. A staff request for a seed is an impostor.
ENDNOTE

## Inventory examples, unrolled

Spot ETH in self-custody: you can send it if you have gas. Spot ETH on a CEX: you can request withdrawal. ETH-perpetual: you cannot send ETH; you can close a position if the engine allows. Three objects, one ticker in a sentence. Intermediate fails when the sentence wins.

USDT on chain 56 in your EOA is a mapping in a USDT contract. USDT as a CEX row is a company IOU. USDT-perp is a derivative. Paying Intermediate in USDT BEP-20 on checkout is a **payment**, not a spot long on Crystal Stones. Different objects again.

## What “I am in CST” can mean, and why this school uses none of them as homework

It can mean a BEP-20 balance at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00`. It can mean a CEX row. It can mean a perp. It can mean a sentence. This academy’s assigned relationship is **verify-only** on chain 56. Not a long. Not a short. Not a farm.

TABLE
Sentence | Object | This school
“I hold CST in MetaMask” | BEP-20 mapping | Verify 0x; no size assigned
“I have CST on an exchange” | IOU | Not homework
“I longed CST 10x” | Perp | Refused
“CST is the play” | Story | Refused
ENDTABLE

## Why a candle cannot be inventory

A candle has no `balanceOf`. It cannot be withdrawn. It cannot be frozen as a row (the venue can halt the pair; that is not the candle). Treating a green candle as “now I have the asset” is how IOU and perp get mashed into spot. If you cannot name the mapping or the company row, you do not have inventory. You have a picture.

## Say this out loud

- Spot is inventory now, not a prophecy.
- One ticker can be a wallet row, a company IOU, or a perpetual.
- A candle is history on one venue.
- Crystal Stones as a sentence is not a long from this school.
- Mentor naming a target is a malfunction.

lessons.title: Bid, ask, spread
lessons.content:
# Bid, ask, spread

A market is a place where resting interest meets taking interest. The **bid** is a rest to acquire inventory at a stated price. The **ask** (offer) is a rest to dispose of inventory at a stated price. The **spread** is the gap. You do not get the mid. The mid is a cartoon drawn between two rests.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to read size-at-the-inside and explain why a one-tick quote on tiny size is a trap for a large taker order.

## Rest, not a feeling

On a central limit order book, a bid is an order the matching engine is willing to store. Until it matches, it is a request. The engine may cancel it. The poster may cancel it. A halt may freeze it. “I had a bid there” is a memory, not a fill.

The **inside bid** is the highest rest still alive. The **inside ask** is the lowest rest still alive. **Size at the inside** is how many units sit at those two prices. A screenshot of the prices without the sizes is half a quote.

## Size at the inside is the quote

Worked case. Inside bid $1.00 × 200 units. Inside ask $1.01 × 200 units. Spread is one tick. A taker order for 5,000 units is not filled at $1.01. It walks: it eats $1.01 × 200, then the next ask, then the next, until 5,000 are done or the order ends. Average fill is worse than the cartoon. Slippage is not an accident. It is the walk.

If the book beyond the inside is empty or spoofed, the walk is a cliff. Thin books advertise tight spreads the way empty shops advertise “open.”

TABLE
Term | Meaning | Failure if ignored
Bid | Rest to acquire at a price | You treat a vanished rest as a floor
Ask | Rest to dispose at a price | You treat a vanished rest as a ceiling
Spread | Ask minus bid | You treat mid as a fill
Size at inside | Units at those two prices | You send 5,000 into 200
Walk | Eating successive levels | You screenshot the first tick
ENDTABLE

## Crossing versus posting

A **taker** removes rest. A **maker** adds rest. Crossing means you pay the spread (and usually the taker fee). Posting means you wait, you may not fill, and you may be the size someone else walks.

On an automated market maker there is no bid wall and no ask wall. The **curve** is the book. Every size has a worse price than the last infinitesimal. Impact replaces the walk. The UI’s “price” is a quote for a tiny size, not a covenant for yours.

## Mid is a cartoon

Mid = (inside bid + inside ask) / 2. Useful as a label. Useless as a promise. Last price is also a label: it is the last match, which may have been 1 unit. Mark and index are later lessons. None of them is your fill until the engine or the pool prints **your** match.

DIAGRAM
BID rest (size)  | spread |  ASK rest (size)
                 ^
                mid (not a fill)
taker walk --> eats ask size, then next, then next
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
This lesson does not assign a pair, a size, or a “tight-spread” hunt. A quote without size is not a quote. The academy will not congratulate you for crossing a one-tick market that had $200 of inventory.
ENDNOTE

## Size at the inside, not only the prices

A 1-tick spread on huge size is a deep book. A 1-tick spread on $200 of size is a trap for a $5,000 market order. Always read **size at the inside**, not only the prices. Thin insides print a pretty spread and a terrible fill.

## One-tick books and screenshot culture

Screenshots crop size. A cropped book is advertising. If you cannot see depth, you cannot cite the spread as a cost. On an AMM there is no bid/ask wall; the spread is the curve versus mid plus fee. Do not paste an AMM screenshot into a “tight spread” argument.

DIAGRAM
ASK 101  size 200
ASK 100  size 50   <- inside ask
--------- spread
BID  99  size 40   <- inside bid
BID  98  size 10
A market buy of 300 walks the asks. The last print is not 100.
ENDDIAGRAM

## Walking the book, with numbers

Inside ask 100 × 50 units, next 101 × 200. A market buy of 80 units takes 50 at 100 and 30 at 101. Average is not 100. The last print may show 101. People then say “it trades at 101.” They bought 80. The remaining ask is thinner. Spread after the walk is a different object than spread before. Quote both or quote neither.

## Mid is not a fill

(bid+ask)/2 is a drawing. Your market buy fills at asks. Your market sell fills at bids. Citing mid as “the price” is how people omit spread from the fee stack. Write inside sizes. If sizes are missing, the spread is a costume.

## Say this out loud

- Bid is rest to acquire; ask is rest to dispose.
- Spread is a cost of crossing, not a decoration.
- Size at the inside is part of the quote.
- A 5,000-unit taker into 200 units walks the book.
- Mid is a cartoon.

lessons.title: Fees you will actually pay
lessons.content:
# Fees you will actually pay

A screenshot of “+40%” that omits fees is fan art. The venue does not care that the candle was pretty. It charges a stack: trading fee, spread or impact, gas or withdrawal, and — on perpetuals — funding. Tiny accounts that match often are not “active.” They are tuition to the matching engine.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name the fee stack on a book and on a pool, and to reject a maker-rebate story as a personality or a business plan.

## The stack, named

**Trading fee.** On a book: maker and taker schedules, often in basis points of notional. On a pool: a pool fee (for example 0.05%, 0.30%, 1.00%) taken from the swap. VIP tiers change book fees. They do not change physics.

**Spread or impact.** The cost of crossing, or of moving a curve. Not a line-item on some receipts. Still a cost.

**Gas.** On a decentralised venue, paid in the **native coin of that chain**. On BSC, that is BNB. Gas is not “the token you acquired.” A failed transaction can still burn gas.

**Withdrawal fee.** A company may charge a flat or percentage fee to send a chain transaction. The chain’s gas is inside their cost. You also wait in their queue.

**Funding.** On perpetuals, a periodic payment between longs and shorts. Not a trading fee. It can dominate if you sit.

**FX and on-ramp.** If units entered through a local-currency rail, conversion and the on-ramp’s spread sit under the first crypto fee. Ignoring them does not delete them.

## Maker rebate is a schedule

Some books pay a rebate to makers and charge takers. That is a published schedule, often with volume tiers, sometimes with a spread-maker requirement. It is not a personality. It is not a business plan this school assigns. Rebate minus spread minus cancels minus adverse selection can be negative. People who treat “I am a maker” as a job title skip that arithmetic.

Worked case. Notional $1,000. Taker fee 0.10% = $1. Spread crossed 0.20% = $2. Withdrawal later $1. Round-trip trading costs before any price change: you already spent more than “a couple of ticks.” Do the same ten times in a week on a tiny account and the venue has a student.

TABLE
Cost | Where it lives | Hidden in a +40% poster?
Maker/taker or pool fee | Schedule or pool | Often
Spread / impact | Book or curve | Almost always
Gas | Native coin of the chain | DEX posters skip it
Withdrawal | Company schedule | CEX posters skip it
Funding | Perp engine, often every 8 hours | Direction-right posters skip it
ENDTABLE

## Tiny size, frequent matches

A small account that crosses all day is not practising discipline. It is transferring a large fraction of equity to fees. The venue is the only party with a positive expected bill. This course does not assign that behaviour. If you touch a venue at all, the fee stack is part of the object, not an afterthought.

## What a +40% screenshot omitted

Time window. Starting notional. Fees in and out. Funding. Whether the position is still open (unrealised is not a withdrawal). Whether the pair was a thin print. Whether the account is a company IOU. A certificate from this school will not convert that screenshot into net.

DIAGRAM
GROSS MOVE
  - taker/maker or pool fee
  - spread or impact
  - gas or withdrawal
  - funding (if perp)
  = number that may no longer be +40%
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Fee literacy is not a call to match more cheaply. It is a reason the academy keeps the signal box empty. A rebate schedule is not homework. Crystal Stones is not a fee-token this school tells you to farm.
ENDNOTE

## Maker rebates are not an income plan

Some books pay makers. That is a fee schedule, not a business model you should build a personality on. Rebates can reverse. They never make a bad fill good. Taker fee + spread + withdrawal fee is the stack a small account actually pays. A tiny account that trades often is paying tuition to the venue — and it is not this academy’s $10.

## DEX fee stack is different objects

On an AMM: pool fee, gas, possible referral, possible aggregator surcharge, possible tax on the token. On a CEX: maker/taker, settlement, withdrawal, spread. Do not compare “0.1%” on one stack to “0.05%” on the other without naming every line.

TABLE
Venue | Lines you must name
CEX book | maker/taker, spread, withdraw, FX if fiat
AMM | pool fee, impact, gas, token tax, aggregator
Perp | taker, funding, spread, liquidation penalty
ENDTABLE

## Small-account arithmetic

$200 account, 0.1% taker each way, 0.2% round trip, plus spread, plus a $1 withdrawal. Five round trips a week is 1% in taker alone before spread. That is not a strategy problem yet. It is a fee stack. This academy’s $10 USDT tuition is a different fee, paid once for a track, not a licence to churn.

## Withdrawal fee as the last line people skip

A $1 withdrawal on a $30 profit is not rounding. On a $5 scalp it is the trade. Count it before you call something a scalp. DEX analog: gas. A $4 gas on a $6 edge is a donation to validators. Small accounts die here without a villain.

## Say this out loud

- Fees are a stack, not a line.
- Spread and impact are costs even when the receipt is quiet.
- DEX gas is the native coin of that chain.
- Maker rebate is a schedule, not a personality.
- A +40% screenshot without fees is incomplete.

# Refusals

This course is a map of venues and kill switches. It is not a desk. If you came for entries, leverage invites, or a weekly ticker, you are in the wrong building. The refusal list is the product. Literacy without a refusal list becomes someone else’s inventory.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to recite what this academy will not send, and to treat a Mentor price target as a malfunction rather than a gift.

## Empty signal box

No pair homework. No candle homework. No “watch this level.” No “easy 2%.” No CST as a trade. Checkout is **USDT BEP-20 payment**, not a long. A certificate is academic. It is not a broker licence, a futures permit, or a VIP tier.

If Mentor — the in-app assistant — ever names a ticker target, a leverage, or an entry, that is **not curriculum**. It is a malfunction. Close the thread. Do not size it. Staff who impersonate a desk in chat are to be treated as hostile until the live site, typed by you, says otherwise.

## This course does not require a trade

You can finish every quiz without matching on a book or a pool. If you insist on touching a venue, the only honest size is money you can lose without writing a recovery narrative. That is not an assignment. It is a boundary. Lab size is still a loss when it vanishes.

API keys with **withdraw** enabled are a theft product. Trade-only keys are still a theft product with extra steps. This school does not ask for either.

## Certificates, XP, and desks that do not exist

Academy XP is not a trading desk. A rank is not a blotter. A Telegram that claims to be “Crystal Stones signals” is not this course. Paid “alpha” belongs in a later module’s refuse pile. There is no academy OTC. There is no admin who needs your 2FA to “verify a fill.”

TABLE
Ask | This school | Not this school
A map of spot / IOU / perp | Yes | A target on any ticker
Fee stack, book vs AMM | Yes | “Easy 2%”
Kill switches, freezes, theatre | Yes | Mentor as broker
$10 USDT BEP-20 checkout | Yes | Pay-in-CST-to-unlock-signals
Empty signal box | Yes | Weekly calls
ENDTABLE

## How a malfunction looks

A chat card: “CST long, target +2%.” A voice note: “Use 10x, stop at the yellow line.” A screenshot of a candle with a rectangle drawn on it, captioned as homework. All three are refusals. The correct operational response is to stop, not to argue the rectangle.

DIAGRAM
REQUEST --> is it a named object / fee / failure mode?
        |-- yes: lesson
        +-- no, it is a target / entry / leverage invite: malfunction
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
If a person or a bot claiming academy staff asks you to open a position, send CST, or share a seed to “unlock trading module 4,” that is not staff. Real checkout is $10 USDT BEP-20. Real Crystal Stones work in this track is verify-only.
ENDNOTE

## Why Mentor must stay mute on entries

A model trained on lesson text will still try to be helpful. Helpful plus a chart is a desk. If Mentor ever gives a ticker target, it is a malfunction. Do not obey malfunctions with size. Report it. The empty box includes Crystal Stones, BTC, and whatever is loud this week.

## This course does not require a trade

You can finish Intermediate without placing an order. Optional tiny tests, if you insist, are money you can lose without a story. Prefer not to. Prefer reading a book and an explorer. Homework is naming objects.

## What a refusal looks like in a chat

Someone posts a CST or BTC target and tags you. The literate reply is not a counter-target. It is: object (spot, IOU, perp), venue, fuse, and “this school does not assign that.” If you cannot name the object, you are not ready to refuse — you are ready to reread Module 1. Helpful counter-calls are still a desk.

## Helpful Mentor, refused

If a chat with the academy voice says “small long on the breakout,” it is off-syllabus. The correct student move is not to scale in “just 1%.” It is to treat the line as a malfunction. 1% is still a desk. Homework remains: name the object, name the fuse, place no order.

## Say this out loud

- The signal box is empty on purpose.
- Mentor naming a target is a malfunction.
- This course does not require a trade.
- A certificate is not a licence.
- “Easy 2%” is a refusal, not a drill.

modules.title: Order books versus AMMs
modules.description: Two matching engines. Two ways to get a bad fill.

lessons.title: The book
lessons.content:
# The book

A **central limit order book** is a list of resting orders plus a matching engine — a company computer — that pairs them with incoming orders under published priority rules. It is not a law of nature. It is software on a machine you do not run. When the machine stops, the list is a picture of what used to be rest.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to describe queue priority, partial fills, and why “I had a bid there” is not a fill.

## Resting orders and the engine

A **limit order** names a price and a size and waits. A **market order** names a size (sometimes a notional) and takes whatever opposite rest exists, usually until filled or a protection limit. The engine’s job is to match: same instrument, opposite sides, prices that cross, under **price-time** priority on most crypto books (better price first; at the same price, earlier rest first).

You do not see the whole list. **Hidden** and **iceberg** orders exist on many venues. Depth charts are incomplete. One venue’s book is not the world’s book.

## Queue priority and partial fills

Worked case. You rest a bid at $10.00 for 100 units. Ahead of you: 400 units at $10.00. A sell of 350 units arrives. Those 350 match the queue ahead. You still have 100 resting and zero fills. A later sell of 50 units fills 50 of yours. You now have a **partial fill** of 50, 50 still resting. The UI that paints the whole 100 as “working” without showing filled-versus-open is lying by compression.

Cancels are first-class. The 400 ahead may vanish before the next sell. Then you are first. Or your own 50 remainder may vanish in a cancel you did not mean (fat-finger, app refresh, kill-switch). The engine’s truth is its log, not your intention.

TABLE
Event | What the engine did | What a screenshot may imply
Rest bid 100 at 10.00 | Enqueued behind older 10.00 size | “I am the bid”
Incoming sell 350 | Filled the queue ahead | “My bid held”
Incoming sell 50 | Partial fill 50 | “Filled” or “not filled,” both wrong
Cancel of remainder | 50 dead | “I still have a bid there”
Matching engine halt | Nothing matches | “The market is the last candle”
ENDTABLE

## Maker, taker, and the walk

**Maker** adds rest that is stored. **Taker** removes rest. Fees often differ. A marketable limit — a “limit” priced so it can match immediately — is a taker even if the button said limit.

A large taker **walks**: it consumes the inside, then the next level, then the next. Average price is a function of displayed (and hidden) size, not of the last print. If you cannot name the size at the first three opposite levels, you cannot name the fill.

## “I had a bid there” is not a fill

A rest that did not match did not transact. Being in the queue is not inventory. Being in the queue during a gap is not protection. Self-trade prevention, post-only rejects, and self-match rules can also prevent a fill you thought was obvious.

DIAGRAM
TIME -->  rest A (older)  rest B (you)  rest C (newer)
INCOMING TAKER eats A first
partial: B may fill later, or cancel, or sit through a halt
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
This academy does not assign resting orders as homework. Learning the queue is so you stop treating a depth chart as a covenant. A company computer can drop your rest without a hearing.
ENDNOTE

## Queue priority

At a price, earlier rest usually fills first. You cannot see your place in some UIs. Partial fills exist. “I had a bid there” is not a fill. Hidden orders and icebergs exist on some company books. You are not seeing physics. You are seeing a matching engine’s policy.

## Market versus limit, said as inventory

A market order takes rest inventory now at whatever prices the walk requires. A limit order joins rest and may never become a fill. Stop-market is a request to become a market when a trigger prints. None of these is a covenant with the universe.

## Partial fills and cancel-replace

Your limit of 100 units at 99 may fill 12 and rest 88. The UI may still draw 100 until it refreshes. Cancel-replace loses queue priority on many engines. “I was first” is not a fact you can see. Write fills from the fill tape, not from the order ticket you meant.

## What the matching engine is allowed to hide

Icebergs, hidden mid-point, post-only rejects, self-trade prevention. Company books are policies. You will not reverse-engineer them from a classroom. You will not assume the drawn wall is the whole rest. You will size as if the wall can vanish — or you will not size, which this school prefers.

## Say this out loud

- The book is rest plus a company matching engine.
- Price-time priority means older same-price rest fills first.
- A partial fill is a fact; a screenshot of the intended size is not.
- Hidden orders mean displayed depth is incomplete.
- “I had a bid there” is not a fill.

Next: AMM as a book with a formula.

lessons.title: AMM as a book with a formula
lessons.content:
# AMM as a book with a formula

An automated market maker does not store a list of human rests at prices. It stores **reserves** and a **function**. The function names a price for every size. Your swap is a transaction that moves the reserves now, or it **reverts**. There is no “leave a bid on the chain” unless a separate limit-layer contract exists, and that contract is another object with its own failure modes.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to contrast impact with spread, and to recall that x·y=k is a curve you already met in DeFi — not a safety rating.

## Reserves plus a function

Classic constant-product: x · y = k. Token X reserve times token Y reserve stays (approximately) constant across a swap, ignoring fees. Larger X in means less Y out per extra unit. That declining Y-per-X **is** the book. Concentrated-liquidity designs change which portion of the curve is active; they do not restore a human rest list.

Fee is usually taken from the input or from the invariant. Liquidity-provider inventory sits in the pool contract. You met that person in the DeFi course. Here you are the taker who moves the curve.

## Fill is now or revert

On a book, a limit can sit. On a plain AMM swap, the transaction either executes inside your slippage bound or the EVM undoes the swap (you still paid gas). Slippage settings are **your worst acceptable execution versus the quote at send time**. They are not a promise that the quote will still be there. Mempool observers can insert transactions before yours. That is sandwiching — later module — not a rounding error.

A specialised **limit-order contract** on top of a pool is extra bytecode. It can fail to fill, fail to refund, or get paused. Do not import book intuition onto a pool without reading whether a limit layer even exists.

TABLE
Book | AMM pool
Rest at a price until cancel | Function of reserves; no rest unless extra contract
Partial fills along a queue | One transaction: in-bound or revert
Spread from two insides | Impact from size versus depth of the curve
Hidden orders possible | k and reserves are visible on-chain
Matching engine can halt | pause() only if the code has it
ENDTABLE

## Impact versus spread

Spread on a book is the gap between insides **before** you walk. Impact is how much worse the average gets **as** you take size. On an AMM the quote for 1 unit can look excellent while the quote for 10,000 units is a different number. UIs that show a price without a size are repeating the mid-cartoon in curve clothing.

Worked case. Pool: 100,000 of token A and 100,000 of token B, fee ignored for the sketch. Spot is 1:1. A swap of 10,000 A in does not return 10,000 B. Constant product: 100,000 × 100,000 = 110,000 × y_new → y_new ≈ 90,909. B out ≈ 9,091. Impact is about 9% versus the 1:1 cartoon. Thin pools punish size. That is the mechanism, not a vendetta.

DIAGRAM
x * y = k
swap moves along the curve
small size ~ quoted slope
large size ~ much worse slope
revert if limit / slippage bound missed
ENDDIAGRAM

## What this academy refuses to do with a curve

No “this pool is the play.” No CST pair as a lab. Reading `getReserves` (or the equivalent) is literacy. Moving the curve is not homework. If you do it anyway, the slippage bound is part of the object you signed.

NOTE
An AMM is public bytecode plus reserves, not a company feeling. It still does not make a ticker honest. Verify Crystal Stones on chain 56 if you are verifying a BEP-20; do not treat a CST/B pool as an assignment.
ENDNOTE

## Limit orders on AMMs are extra programs

Some protocols add on-chain limit layers. They are extra contracts (gas, admin, another allowance). Until you read them, assume an AMM fill is **now or revert**, not a resting bid. Aggregators that promise “limit on DEX” are wrapping that extra program or a company order.

## x·y=k impact, one line you must be able to say

Buying Δx of X from a pool with reserves x, y moves the price. Large Δx versus x is the cost. A 0.3% fee is not the whole cost. People quote the fee and ignore impact because the fee is a round number. Impact is the curve. Token taxes sit on top if present.

## Deadline and slippage as the rest of the order type

An AMM swap is not “at the mid.” You set `amountOutMin` and a deadline. Too tight, revert (you still paid gas). Too loose, a searcher takes the gap. That pair of numbers is your order type. 15% slippage because “it failed once” is how you fund sandwiches. Review DeFi course if this paragraph is new; here it is the book-shaped cost.

## Say this out loud

- An AMM is reserves plus a function, not a rest list.
- Fill is now or revert, unless an extra limit-layer contract exists.
- Impact is the book; the 1-unit quote is not your size’s quote.
- x·y=k is a curve, not a safety rating.
- Slippage is your worst acceptable execution, not a covenant.

Next: where the inventory sits.

lessons.title: Where the inventory sits
lessons.content:
# Where the inventory sits

“I have 1,000 units” is not a location. Location is the fact that decides whether a freeze, a bug, or a withdrawal queue can touch you. On a centralised venue the units sit in **company wallets** (hot, cold, custodial partners) and you sit in a **row**. On a decentralised pool the units sit in a **contract**, then — after a swap — in **your** address if the transaction succeeded.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name those two locations and to treat a proof-of-reserves screenshot as something other than a full liability audit.

## CEX: company wallets, your row

A spot balance on a company app is an IOU. The matching engine debits and credits rows. The chain moves when the company **withdraws** to an address, or when someone deposits. Between those events, explorers do not show your name. Internal transfers between two usernames on the same venue often **never hit the chain**.

**Proof of reserves** is usually a snapshot of some wallets the company wants to display, sometimes with a merkle tree of customer claims. It is not automatically a proof of **all** liabilities, off-balance derivatives, pending withdrawals, or affiliated entities. A green dashboard is a marketing object until you can read what was hashed and what was omitted.

## DEX: the pool, then your wallet

On a swap, inventory leaves the pool mapping and appears in yours in the same transaction (plus fee to LPs, plus gas). On providing liquidity, inventory leaves yours and sits in the pool (or in an NFT/position manager). You already know LP risk from DeFi: the pool can be drained if the bytecode or the admin key allows it. There is no ticket form.

Self-custody after a swap is still self-custody: the next phishing site can ask you to `approve` the new tokens away. Location changed. Responsibility did not evaporate.

TABLE
Location | Who signs a send | What “balance” means | Explorer
Your EOA / contract wallet | You | Token mapping or native | Yes, on that chain
Pool contract | The pool’s code + caller | Reserves | Yes
CEX row | The company | IOU | No, until withdraw
CEX hot/cold wallets | The company | Pooled customer inventory | Wallets, not your row
ENDTABLE

## Withdraw a test if you need the fact of control

If the question is “can I actually move this IOU onto a chain I named,” the empirical method is a **tiny test withdrawal** to an address you control, on the network you meant, with the memo/tag if any. Then size. Help desks do not unwrite a wrong-network send because a school asked. This is operations, not a trade assignment.

Worked case. Row shows 500 USDT. Test withdraw 12 USDT on BSC (chain 56) to your address. Explorer shows the hash, the token contract, and the incoming mapping. Only then is “I can withdraw USDT on 56” a fact. A screenshot of the row was never that fact.

DIAGRAM
[POOL] --swap tx--> [YOUR WALLET]
[COMPANY WALLETS] --withdraw request--> queue --> chain tx --> [YOUR WALLET]
[COMPANY WALLETS] --internal send--> [another row]   (no chain)
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Proof-of-reserves is not a reason this academy names a favourite venue. It is a document with a scope. If you cannot state the scope, you saw a poster. The academy will not re-credit a CEX row.
ENDNOTE

## Proof of reserves theatre

A CEX hashing wallets is not a full liability audit. It can still be useful. It does not make a database row into an EOA you control. Withdraw a test if you need the fact of control. Do not treat a PoR page as spot in your wallet.

## On-chain, the inventory is the pair or the vault

AMM reserves sit in the pair/vault contract. Your “spot” after a swap sits in your EOA’s token mapping. Your LP sits in an LP token mapping. Three places. A dashboard that shows one number has mashed them.

## Three wallets, one screenshot

A dashboard shows “$12,000 spot.” It may be: CEX row, DEX wallet via a connected EOA, and an LP position priced at a stale ratio. Click through to the 0x or the venue. If you cannot land on one object, the screenshot is mashed. Mashed inventory is how people think they can withdraw what is actually a perp or an LP share.

## Withdraw test as the only PoR that is yours

A $20 withdrawal to an EOA you control, confirmed on the explorer, is the fact of control for that $20. A hashed-wallet page is a company poster. Do not skip the test and then argue about reserve attestations. Also: the test costs fees. Optional. Not assigned. Prefer reading to testing if you do not need the fact.

## Say this out loud

- A CEX spot balance is usually a company ledger IOU.
- DEX swap inventory sits in the pool, then in your wallet if the tx succeeds.
- Proof-of-reserves is not a full liability audit.
- Internal username sends may never hit the chain.
- A tiny test withdraw is how you check control, not a waste.

Next: venue choice is risk choice.

lessons.title: Venue choice is risk choice
lessons.content:
# Venue choice is risk choice

Picking a venue is picking a **failure mode**. A company fails in courts, freezes, outages, and insolvency queues. A pool fails in bytecode, admin keys, oracles, and the absence of a form to fill. This school will not pick your venue. It will insist you name the failure you can tolerate instead of the logo you can recite.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to list custody, matching engine, fees, and withdraw path as four named choices — not a hymn.

## Company failure is paperwork and queues

A centralised venue is a legal person. It can halt matching. It can freeze a row because of KYC, a sanctions list, a duplicate account, or a risk-engine flag. It can be late on withdrawals while still showing a balance. Courts may eventually speak. “Eventually” is not a trading session. If you need fiat on-ramps, you bought that product — including its paperwork.

Outages are not theoretical. An engine that is down cannot honour a stop, a cancel, or a close. Your row is still a row.

## Pool failure is bytecode and silence

A pool does not have a complaints department that can reverse a confirmed transaction. If `pause()` exists, an admin can freeze the curve. If it does not, the curve keeps quoting through a crisis, often thin, often unusable for size. Drains, infinite-mint tokens, and hostile fee switches are DeFi objects. You do not file a PDF at the pool.

Bridges between company and chain are a **third** animal: wrong network, fake deposit address, delayed attestation. Naming two venues without naming the bridge is how people donate.

TABLE
Choice | Company venue | Pool venue
Custody | IOU until withdraw | Code plus your key
Halt | Policy, button, incident | Only if coded (pause)
Reverse a confirmed send | Ticket, maybe | No
Freeze you | Yes, as a feature | Only via your signature or the token’s own blacklist if it has one
Who to call | Support, then courts | Nobody useful
ENDTABLE

## Four names, then a venue

1. **Custody** — IOU or self-custody.
2. **Engine** — book or curve (or hybrid).
3. **Fees** — the stack from module 1.
4. **Withdraw path** — asset, chain ID, token contract, memo/tag.

If any of the four is “whatever the app defaulted,” you did not choose. You inherited a risk. This course still does not name a best exchange. Quizzes that offer a brand as the answer are wrong on purpose.

DIAGRAM
LOGO
  |-- custody?
  |-- engine?
  |-- fee stack?
  +-- withdraw path (asset, chain ID, contract, memo)?
missing a name = inherited failure
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy support cannot choose a venue for you and cannot unwind a public chain or a company ledger. Pick the failure you can tolerate. Do not pick a hymn. Do not pick Crystal Stones as a required pair.
ENDNOTE

## Jurisdiction versus bytecode

A company is in a place with courts and regulators. That can help you or freeze you. A pool is in bytecode. That can drain you without a form to fill. Pick with the failure you can tolerate, not the logo you like.

## This academy is not a venue

Checkout is a payment. It is not a spot venue for CST. Do not treat a successful Intermediate payment as evidence that a pair is a good place to trade. Different objects.

## Failure you can tolerate, written as a pick

Pick A: company freeze, KYC, possible bail-in, human support that may not help. Pick B: bytecode drain, no freeze, no support, explorer as the record. Pick C: mix (deposit on CEX, withdraw to EOA, swap on AMM). C doubles the doors. This school will not pick for you. It will not let you pretend you picked none.

## Mixing doors on purpose

Deposit fiat on a CEX (freeze door), withdraw USDT on chain 56 (wrong-network door), swap on an AMM (allowance door). Each hop is a chosen failure. Write the hops before you call it “simple on-ramp.” This academy checkout is one hop: USDT BEP-20 on the named page. Do not add hops “for class.”

## Say this out loud

- Venue choice is risk choice.
- Companies fail as freezes, courts, and outages.
- Pools fail as bytecode, and there is no form.
- Name custody, engine, fees, and withdraw path.
- This course names no best exchange.

modules.title: Leverage is a loan with a kill switch
modules.description: Perpetuals, margin, liquidation, funding. Not homework.

lessons.title: Margin and maintenance
lessons.content:
# Margin and maintenance

**Leverage** is a loan that lets a small cash pile control a larger **notional**. The venue (or a protocol) is the lender. **Initial margin** is what the engine demands to open. **Maintenance margin** is the floor. Below it, **liquidation** is a function: the engine sells or closes you, usually with a penalty, on **its** mark. This course does not assign leverage. The arithmetic is the object.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to compute an isolated 10x notional and show why a ~10% adverse mark can erase the box before fees.

## Isolated 10x, in numbers

Isolated box: $1,000 margin. Leverage 10x. Notional = $10,000. If the mark moves ~10% against the position, unrealised loss ≈ $1,000. The box is gone. Maintenance is usually **above** zero, so the engine does not wait for a perfect 10%. Fees, funding, and a gap can take you earlier. A 5% adverse move at 10x is already a 50% dent in the margin — not a cushion of 50% safety.

Gaps skip pretty lines. The next mark after an outage can be through the maintenance line. Isolated means the **declared** box is the fuel. It does not mean the venue cannot bill a leftover in some rulebooks (auto-deleveraging, insurance funds, clawback — venue-specific). Read the venue’s function. Do not import a folk tale.

TABLE
Margin | Leverage | Notional | Rough adverse mark that consumes isolated margin (before fees)
$1,000 | 5x | $5,000 | ~20%
$1,000 | 10x | $10,000 | ~10%
$1,000 | 20x | $20,000 | ~5%
$1,000 | 50x | $50,000 | ~2%
ENDTABLE

## Maintenance is the venue’s line

You do not vote on maintenance. It can differ by contract, by tier, by notional. Liquidation is not a courtesy call. It is code plus an engine plus, on-chain, bots that pay gas to be first. On-chain perps add **contract bugs plus liquidation bots**. That is extra risk versus a company engine, not zero risk.

A UI that paints “liquidation price” as a single number is a summary of a formula you may not have. If you cannot find the formula (mark, maintenance ratio, fees), you cannot name the fuse.

## This is not homework

10x Crystal Stones perps are not assigned. No perp is assigned. If you still open a leveraged box, size as if the kill switch **is** the product — because it is. Revenge-sizing after a liquidation is module 6’s refusal.

DIAGRAM
$1,000 isolated --> 10x --> $10,000 notional
mark -10% (and fees) --> margin ~ 0 --> liquidation function
gap can skip the pretty line
ENDDIAGRAM

Worked remainder. $1,000 isolated, 10x long, taker fee 0.05% on open and on close, plus a 0.3% gap through maintenance. The fee on $10,000 is $5 per side. The gap does not politely stop at your number. The box can print a round-trip that is both a total loss of margin and a surprise remainder, depending on the venue’s bankruptcy rules.

NOTE
Leverage literacy is not a 10x drill. The academy’s trading desk does not exist. A Mentor line that says “use 10x here” is a malfunction. Isolated math exists so you can refuse the cartoon of a safe 5% wiggle.
ENDNOTE

## Isolated math, written slowly

$1,000 isolated on 10× is $10,000 notional. A 10% adverse mark ≈ $1,000 loss ≈ gone, before fees and penalties. The UI showing “$10,000 position” is not $10,000 of yours. Maintenance is a **higher** line than zero; you are liquidated before the isolated box is mathematically empty, because the venue takes a penalty.

## Cross is a shared box

Cross lets winners fund losers in the same account. It also lets one bad mark eat the whole box. That is not courage. It is a setting. This school will not tell you which setting to pick. It will tell you they are different kill switches.

## Isolated box versus the UI notional, recap number

UI: “position $10,000.” Box: $1,000. Notional is borrowed exposure. Teaching yourself to read the box first is the whole lesson. If a screenshot shows only notional, it is advertising leverage, not documenting risk.

## Penalty on top of the line

Liquidation is not a full rebate of remaining box. A penalty pays keepers or the venue. Isolated $1,000 can die with $80 still “there” on a naive spreadsheet. Read liquidation fee. Write it next to maintenance. Courage sentences omit both.

## Say this out loud

- Leverage is a loan with liquidation.
- $1,000 at 10x is $10,000 notional.
- A ~10% adverse mark can consume that isolated box before fees.
- Maintenance is the venue’s line, not yours.
- This course does not assign 10x, including not on CST.

Next: perpetuals are not spot.

lessons.title: Perpetuals are not spot
lessons.content:
# Perpetuals are not spot

A **perpetual swap** is a derivative with no expiry date. It is built to track an **index** of spot prints, using **funding** payments between longs and shorts so the perpetual price does not drift forever. You do not hold the coin. You cannot withdraw the coin. You hold a contract. You can close if the engine (or the protocol) still accepts closes.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate a perp from spot inventory, and to treat funding as a meter that can bleed you while you are “right” on direction.

## Tracking an index, not owning a unit

Spot self-custody: a mapping you can transfer. Spot IOU: a row you can request as a withdraw. Perp: a position size, an entry mark, an unrealised PnL, a margin. Settling to cash (or a stable IOU) is the usual design. Delivering the coin is not.

If the venue dies, your PnL is a row in a dead database, or a claim in a court, or — on-chain — whatever the remaining bytecode still allows. That is counterparty or contract risk, not “I still have the coins in the wallet.”

## Funding is a periodic transfer

On many venues, **positive funding** means longs pay shorts; negative means shorts pay longs. The sign is a convention you must read per venue, not a folk song. The economic idea: if the perp trades above the index, make longs pay so they have a reason to close and shorts a reason to open, tugging the perp back. The opposite when cheap.

Interval is **often eight hours**, three times a day. It is not universal. Some venues use one hour or another clock. Sitting through eight-hour prints while “right” on direction can still bleed a large fraction of a tight box.

Worked case. Notional $10,000. Funding +0.01% per eight-hour print, three prints a day. Long pays ≈ $1 per print, ≈ $3/day, ≈ $90/30 days if the rate stays. On a $1,000 isolated box that is 9% of margin in a month **without** the mark moving against you. Direction right, meter wrong.

TABLE
Object | Holds the coin? | Withdraw the coin? | Extra meter
Self-custody spot | Yes (mapping) | Yes, if you can sign | Gas
CEX spot IOU | Company does | If they send it | Withdrawal fee, freeze
Perpetual | No | No | Funding + liquidation
ENDTABLE

## Right direction, still bleed

Funding is not a fee you negotiate. It is a transfer between sides. High positive funding on a crowded long is how the late crowd pays the other side to exist. This course does not assign a funding farm. It names the meter so a green mark does not fool you into calling the account “up.”

DIAGRAM
INDEX (spot basket)
   ^
   |  funding tug
PERP MARK
position = derivative; close if engine allows
no coin out the withdraw door
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
A perpetual is not a warehouse receipt. Academy XP will not pay your funding. CST perps are not homework. If a chat promises “funding is free yield,” that is a farm story, and this school does not assign farms.
ENDNOTE

## Funding sign

If funding is positive, longs pay shorts on many venues. You can hold a long that is “right” and still bleed. Read the funding interval (8h is common, not universal). Funding is not interest from a bank. It is a payment between accounts so the perp does not drift too far from index — until it does.

## You cannot withdraw the coin from a perp

There is no `transfer` of the underlying from a perpetual position. Close, then you have company-row cash or collateral. Then you may withdraw, if the company allows. That chain of requests is not spot.

## Close is a request on a company engine

In a halt, in an outage, or when mark has already run, “close” may not be available. Spot in an EOA can still `transfer` if the token is not paused and you have gas. That difference is why mash sentences kill accounts. You cannot withdraw ETH from a BTC-perp. You cannot send CST from a CST-perp. There is no CST-perp homework here anyway.

## Funding as a clock, not a vibe

Interval 8 hours is common. Rate can flip sign. A week of being “right” with a bad sign is a bleed that looks like incompetence and is actually a clock. Screenshot PnL without funding is a cropped book. Still not a reason to open a CST perp — refused.

## Say this out loud

- A perpetual holder holds a derivative, not the spot asset.
- You cannot withdraw the coin from a perp.
- Funding tethers the perp toward an index by paying between sides.
- On many venues positive funding means longs pay shorts.
- The interval is often eight hours, not a law of the universe.

Next: isolated versus cross margin.

lessons.title: Isolated versus cross margin
lessons.content:
# Isolated versus cross margin

**Isolated** boxes a position: the declared margin is the fuel, and (in the advertised design) death stays in the box. **Cross** makes the **account** the fuel: several positions, and often the spot bag sitting on the same derivatives wallet, share a fuse. Efficiency is the marketing word for shared fuse.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain how a spot bag plus a short perpetual on cross can liquidate **both** when marks diverge, and why UI defaults are design rather than friendship.

## Isolated boxes the fuse

You allocate $800 to one contract. Liquidation eats toward that $800. Other isolated boxes, in theory, remain. You still have to read whether the venue can tap other balances in bankruptcy, insurance events, or auto-deleveraging. Isolated is a **box**, not a treaty with the universe.

Adding margin to an isolated position is a choice that enlarges the box. Removing margin shrinks it and moves the fuse closer. People do both in a hurry. Hurry is module 6.

## Cross is one fuse

Cross: unrealised loss on position A reduces collateral available for position B. A spike in A’s mark can liquidate B even if B’s own story is “fine.” If the account also holds spot inventory as collateral, that spot is fuel. You did not open a “spot long.” You posted inventory to a derivatives engine.

Worked case. Account on cross: 2.0 of a coin posted as collateral, marked at $2,000, plus a short perpetual of 1.0 of the same coin at 5x. The coin’s mark rips **up** 15%. The short is in loss. Maintenance fails. The engine liquidates the short **and** can consume the spot collateral that was backing it. The divergence you thought was a hedge was a shared fuse. Hedges on cross are not two boxes. They are one account.

TABLE
Mode | Fuel | Typical advertisement | Failure picture
Isolated | Declared margin for that position | “Risk contained” | Box dies; leftover rules still venue-specific
Cross | Account (and often posted spot) | “More efficient / higher buying power” | One mark can take several objects
Portfolio / special | Venue formula | “Offsets” | Formula you did not read
ENDTABLE

## Defaults are design

Apps default to cross because it looks like more buying power and fewer “transfer to isolated” taps. That is a product choice. It is not your friend. If you cannot see whether an account is cross or isolated **before** a position exists, you do not have a map.

On-chain perp protocols have their own words (cross, isolated, account health). Read health as a function, not as a heart-rate emoji.

DIAGRAM
ISOLATED:  [box A]  [box B]  [spot wallet elsewhere]
CROSS:     [ A + B + posted spot ]  <-- one fuse
short perp + spot bag on CROSS --> both can go when marks diverge
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
This lesson is not an instruction to hedge. A hedge on cross that shares collateral is a single object. The academy will not diagnose your account mode in a DM. If staff ask you to screenshot an API key to “check isolated,” that is an impostor.
ENDNOTE

## Hedge myth

A spot bag and a short perp on cross can be a hedge **or** a way to liquidate both when marks diverge. Basis and funding break neat hedges. Isolated boxes the perp so the spot bag is not automatically fuel. Still not assigned homework.

## Why this school names the setting and stops

Choosing isolated or cross is a risk preference. Education names the kill switch. It does not size the box. Mentor must not say “use 3× cross on CST.” That sentence is a malfunction.

## What cross actually shares

Every position’s unrealised PnL and every collateral coin in that account. A winning ETH-perp can keep a losing alt-perp alive — until ETH mark reverses and both die. Isolated would have killed the alt alone. Neither sentence is “use this.” Both are how the box is wired.

## One account, two fuses, mashed UI

Some UIs show one margin mode in a header and a different mode on the ticket. Confirm per position. A header that says isolated while the ticket is cross is how people donate a spot bag they thought was boxed. Screenshot both before you believe either. Prefer not to need the screenshot because you are not sized.

## Say this out loud

- Isolated boxes the position’s fuel.
- Cross: the account backs multiple positions — shared fuse.
- Spot posted as collateral is fuel, not a separate safe bag.
- A spot bag plus a short perp on cross can liquidate both.
- UI defaults are design, not a friend.

Next: stop orders are requests.

lessons.title: Stop orders are requests
lessons.content:
# Stop orders are requests

A **stop** is an instruction: if a trigger price trades (or a mark prints), then send a market or a limit. It is not a covenant with the universe. Gaps skip limits. Engine outages skip both. On-chain, a stop is a transaction that must be mined, or a keeper network that must show up. Neither is physics.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to contrast stop-market with stop-limit, and to refuse the sentence “I had a stop so I was safe.”

## Stop-market versus stop-limit

**Stop-market.** When the trigger prints, the engine submits a **market** order (or a marketable sweep). You prioritise getting out over price. In a gap, you may fill far beyond the trigger. That is the point of a market: it walks whatever rest exists. If rest is gone, you get whatever the engine’s protection rules allow — including a reject, a partial, or a horrific average.

**Stop-limit.** When the trigger prints, the engine submits a **limit** at your specified price. If the market has already gapped through that limit, the order **rests or does nothing useful**. You prioritised price over exit. You may still be in the position. People draw stop-limits on candles and call it risk management. It is a wish with a price cap.

TABLE
Type | After trigger | Gap through your number | Outage
Stop-market | Sweep / market | Fill may be far worse | Instruction never runs
Stop-limit | Limit rest at your cap | May not fill at all | Instruction never runs
Hard-coded on-chain close | Needs a mined tx / keeper | Depends on gas and bots | Chain congestion equals delay
Mental stop | Nothing | Nothing | Nothing
ENDTABLE

## Gaps and outages

A candle with no prints in the middle is a gap. Your trigger was in the blank. The next print is beyond it. Stop-market walks the new book. Stop-limit sits. An engine **outage** means neither instruction is processed. When matching resumes, the mark may already be through maintenance. Liquidation does not wait for your stop to catch up.

Worked case. Isolated long, trigger at 100, stop-limit 99. Next print 94. The limit at 99 does not match a book whose inside is 94. Position still open. Maintenance at 95. Liquidation function runs. The stop-limit was a rest that never became a fill. “I had a stop there” joins “I had a bid there.”

DIAGRAM
price
 |   trigger
 |     X  <-- gap
 |          new inside
 +------------------> time
stop-limit rests at old cap; stop-market walks new book; outage: neither
ENDDIAGRAM

## Not a covenant

Writing a stop in a notebook is not a protocol. A screenshot of a stop ticket is not a fill. This course still does not assign a position that would need a stop. The literacy is so you do not treat a request as a shield, and so you do not accept “guaranteed scalp with a tight stop” from a paid group.

NOTE
Stops are engine instructions. The academy will not place one for you, will not watch your account, and will not honour a screenshot as a refund request. A recovery DM after a gap is hostile until proven on an origin you typed.
ENDNOTE

## Stop-market versus stop-limit

Stop-market becomes a market when triggered — fill uncertain, especially in a gap. Stop-limit becomes a limit — may not fill in a gap. Neither is a covenant. On-chain, some “stops” are keepers that may not fire. Read whether a human or a bot must be awake.

## Stops on thin CST-class books

A stop on a thin pair can be the print that the theatre wanted. This school still will not assign a CST trade. The sentence is: thin books plus stops are fuel. Leave it as literacy.

## Gaps and the print you did not want

A stop at 90 on a book that last printed 100 does nothing until a print at 90 (or through, depending on the venue). In a gap from 100 to 80, a stop-market becomes a market into 80s. Fill is 80-ish, not 90. Complaining that “the stop was at 90” is naming the request, not the fill. Thin CST-class books gap. Still not an assignment to trade them.

## On-chain keepers

If a “stop” is a bot that must send a tx, then gas spikes, chain halt, or a dead keeper means no stop. That is not a CEX engine. Do not import CEX intuition onto a keeper. Read who calls. If you cannot name the caller, you do not have a stop.

## Say this out loud

- A stop is a request, not physics.
- Stop-market prioritises exit and can fill far beyond trigger.
- Stop-limit prioritises price and can fail to fill in a gap.
- Engine outage skips both.
- “I had a stop” is not a fill.

lessons.title: Deposit and withdraw are network questions
lessons.content:
# Deposit and withdraw are network questions

The letters USDT name several contracts on several chains. An exchange deposit screen is a **multiple-choice network question**. You must match **chain ID**, **token contract**, and — on some assets — a **memo or tag**. BNB Smart Chain is **chain ID 56**. Getting any of those three wrong is how a ticker becomes a ticket, or a hole.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to list chain ID, contract, and memo before a send, and to treat an internal username transfer as something that never hit the explorer.

## Chain ID is geography

Ethereum mainnet is 1. BNB Smart Chain is 56. Others exist. Address shapes can look identical. State is not shared. USDT on chain 1 is a row in one contract. USDT on chain 56 is a row in another. Sending “USDT” to an exchange address that expected the other book is a common donation.

The company may publish a recovery ticket for **some** wrong-network deposits, for a fee, on a delay, when they control a key on the accidental chain. They may also say no. Academy support cannot re-credit a wrong-network send. Public pages do not unwind because a school asked.

## Memo, tag, and internal sends

Some deposit addresses are shared. The **memo/tag/payment ID** is how the company credits **your** row. Missing memo: the chain tx succeeded and the company does not know whom to credit. That is not decorative. It is part of the address when the venue says it is.

**Internal** sends (username to username on the same company) often never hit any chain. BscScan will not show them. Do not treat an in-app confirmation as an explorer hash. If you need a hash, you need a withdrawal, not a nickname transfer.

TABLE
Field | Job | Failure
Chain ID | Which book | USDT on 1 to a 56 deposit (or reverse)
Token contract | Which mapping | Lookalike ticker, wrong 0x
Memo/tag | Which customer row | Tx ok, credit missing
Destination address | Who can spend | Poison address, phishing paste
Internal username | Company row to row | Invisible on BscScan — not a chain fact
ENDTABLE

## Tiny then size

A test deposit or test withdraw of a small amount, on the network you meant, is how you check the path. Then size. This is operations. It is not a trade. Help desks are slow. A second panicked send “to make them notice” is a second hole.

Worked case. Intend USDT on BSC to a company deposit. Confirm chain ID 56 in the wallet. Confirm the company’s BSC deposit address (typed, not from a chat). Confirm the token contract the company lists for USDT on BSC. Send 10 USDT. Wait for the **row** to credit, not merely for your outgoing hash. Only then consider size. If the row is silent, stop. Do not repeat.

DIAGRAM
WALLET --?--> VENUE DEPOSIT
check: chain ID (56 for BSC)
     token contract
     memo/tag if any
     address from the real origin you typed
wrong network USDT = ticket or hole
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy support cannot unwrite a public transaction or a company miss-credit. Staff will never ask you to send a “test” to a chat 0x. Checkout remains $10 USDT BEP-20 on the academy page — a payment path, not a deposit to a trading venue we named.
ENDNOTE

## Internal transfers

Some companies let you send to a username. That never hit the chain. It is a row edit. Fast, reversible by them, invisible on BscScan. Do not use an explorer to “prove” an internal send.

## Wrong-network USDT

USDT on Ethereum, USDT on BSC, USDT on another book: different contracts. Depositing BSC-USDT to an ERC-20 deposit address is a support ticket or a hole. Name chain ID 56 before you move USDT for tuition or anything else. Academy checkout expects the network the page names.

## Memo tags and exchange deposit 0x

Some deposits require a memo/tag (a company sub-account). Wrong tag, credit to someone else or a long ticket. The chain 0x was correct; the company row was not. This is not an explorer problem. Also: exchange deposit addresses rotate. Old 0x from a screenshot may be retired. Copy from the logged-in page that day, then check the first and last four.

## First and last four, every time

Clipboard malware swaps the middle of an 0x. Check first four and last four against the page you typed, not against a chat. Exchange deposit 0x included. Academy checkout address included — only the one on the academy origin, never a DM. CST 0x is for verify, not for a deposit.

## Say this out loud

- Ticker is not a network.
- BSC is chain ID 56.
- Memo/tag can be the difference between a credit and a hole.
- Internal username sends may never hit the chain.
- Tiny test, then size; a second panicked send is a second hole.

Next: a company can freeze a row.

lessons.title: A company can freeze a row
lessons.content:
# A company can freeze a row

A centralised venue is a legal person with a risk engine. **Freeze** is a feature: KYC gaps, compliance holds, sanctioned addresses, duplicate accounts, “suspicious activity,” court orders. If you need fiat on-ramps, bank rails, and a password reset desk, you bought that product. Name it at **deposit time**, not at withdrawal-panic time.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to contrast a company freeze with self-custody’s different deaths, and to refuse the fantasy that USDT cannot be frozen because it is “crypto.”

## Freeze is a ledger action

The chain may still show company wallets moving. Your **row** can be locked anyway. You will see a balance that will not send. Support tickets, document uploads, waiting. That is not a chain reorg. It is a company action. USDT as a token can also be blacklisted **at the contract** on some issuers and chains — a separate, issuer-level freeze. Two freeze machines: issuer and venue. Neither is “impossible on USDT.”

Self-custody is not frozen by an exchange risk engine, because there isn’t one. Self-custody is drained by a signed approve or transfer, a seed leak, a phishing site, a hostile token, or a lost key. Different animal. Not a saint.

## Name the product at deposit time

If you cannot tolerate a freeze, do not store life-changing size on a row. If you cannot tolerate self-custody’s silence, do not store life-changing size on a key. Split is a choice, not a slogan. This school still does not pick a venue and still does not assign a size.

TABLE
Event | Company row | Self-custody
KYC hold | Freeze possible | No KYC engine (you still have laws)
Sanctioned counterparty | Freeze / reject | You can still sign; you may still have legal exposure
Password ticket | Recovery theatre, sometimes real | No password; seed is the ticket
Risk-engine flag | Freeze | No such engine
Phishing signature | If they phish the login / API | Direct drain
ENDTABLE

## Suspicious activity is a phrase with a queue

It may mean a real investigation. It may mean a crude heuristic. You will not debug it from a classroom. You will not speed it up by sending CST to an “unfreeze wallet.” That wallet is the scam. Official process lives on an origin **you type**, not in a DM after a loss.

DIAGRAM
DEPOSIT --> row
            |-- withdraw request --> chain (maybe)
            |-- freeze (KYC / compliance / court / risk flag)
            +-- insolvency queue
name this at deposit, not at panic
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Staff never need your 2FA, your selfie next to a handwritten seed, or remote control to “unfreeze an academy-linked account.” There is no such account. Tuition was checkout. Trading venues are not us.
ENDNOTE

## Compliance is the product

If you need fiat on-ramps, you bought freeze-and-KYC as part of the product. Complaining that a freeze exists is like complaining that an AMM has impact. Name it at deposit time.

## Freeze versus pause

A CEX freeze is a company policy on a database row. A token `pause` is bytecode on transfers. A USDT blacklist is a company function on a token. Three doors. Intermediate readers name which door closed, not “crypto is down.”

## What freeze does not unwrite

A freeze on a CEX does not reverse a prior on-chain withdrawal. Once USDT left on chain 56 to an EOA, the company row is gone; the mapping is on the token. Conversely, a freeze can stop a withdrawal you thought was “your USDT.” Name which side of the door you were on. Tuition checkout that has already confirmed is an academy invoice, not a CEX row — different company, still not a seed.

## Freeze after you clicked withdraw

Some venues can still intercept a pending withdraw. Some cannot once the tx is broadcast. You will not memorise every venue. You will read that venue’s docs before you need them. A freeze is not the chain pausing. Do not tweet “BSC is down” because a company button greys.

## Say this out loud

- A CEX freeze is a company action on a ledger row.
- USDT can be frozen by a venue, and sometimes by an issuer blacklist.
- Fiat on-ramps are a product that includes paperwork.
- Self-custody is not drained by an exchange risk engine; it has other deaths.
- Name freeze risk at deposit time.

Next: price is local to the venue.

lessons.title: Price is local to the venue
lessons.content:
# Price is local to the venue

A last price is a print on **that** matching engine or **that** pool. It is not a law. It is not automatically your fill on another venue. Arbitrage usually keeps similar instruments close **until it does not**: halt, depeg, withdrawal pause, oracle lag, thin night books.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate a CEX halt from an AMM that cannot halt unless pause() exists in the code, and to explain why a halted company’s screen is not the world’s price.

## Halts versus curves that do not sleep

A company can **halt** a pair: no matching, last candle frozen, buttons grey. Reasons include volatility, listing incidents, index issues, or operational failure. During a halt, a DEX pool in the same ticker letters may still quote. That quote can run — often on thin reserves — while you cannot move inventory off the company to chase it, because withdrawals may also be paused.

An AMM **cannot halt** unless the bytecode exposes pause() (or a similar switch) and someone calls it. No pause in code means the curve keeps serving whatever inventory remains. That is not heroism. It is the absence of a button. It can be a thin, vicious market.

TABLE
Venue state | Company book | AMM without pause | AMM with pause()
Normal | Local prints | Local curve | Local curve
Halt / pause | No matching | Still quotes | Admin can freeze
Withdrawals paused | IOU stuck | You already had chain inventory or not | Same
Depeg / thin | Local last can lie | Impact explodes | Depends if paused
ENDTABLE

## Last on A is not fill on B

Worked case. Venue A last = 1.00. Venue B pool quotes 0.94 for small size. You do not “have” 0.94 on A. You cannot withdraw from A during a halt. You cannot assume 0.94 is available for your size on B. Three different numbers: A’s last, B’s quote for 1 unit, B’s quote for your size. Arbitrageurs need free inventory, free withdrawals, working rails, and gas. Remove any one and the gap lives.

Index and mark (next module) are yet more local constructions. Do not import a halted company’s last into a perpetual’s liquidation math unless the venue’s formula says it does — and then you have a different problem.

DIAGRAM
VENUE A last  ----halt----  frozen print
VENUE B pool  ----still running----  thin quote
withdraw A --blocked--> cannot move IOU to B
local price != your fill != index
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
This academy does not send you to “trade the halt.” Thin DEX prices during a CEX pause are a picture of trapped inventory, not a homework desk. We will not refund a fill you took because a screenshot of another venue looked better.
ENDNOTE

## Halts

A CEX can halt a pair. An AMM cannot “halt” unless paused in code. During a CEX halt, DEX prices can run. That is not free money; it is often unwithdrawable inventory or thin liquidity. Last print on venue A is not a right to fill on venue B.

## Index versus last versus mark

Last is one fill. Index is a basket some venues compute. Mark is what liquidations use. If you cannot find the mark formula in the venue docs, you do not know your kill switch. Do not lever an undocumented mark.

## Arb is not a free lesson

If venue A prints 10 and venue B prints 11, the difference is not your profit. Withdrawal delays, KYC, gas, impact, and halt risk sit in the middle. This school will not assign arb homework. Literacy is: do not cite A’s last print as B’s fill.

## Last, mark, index — recap card

Last: a fill that happened. Index: a basket, delayed, weighted, venue-defined. Mark: liquidation input. Citing last as mark is how people are surprised by a hunt. Write which integer you mean. Do not lever any of them as homework.

## Say this out loud

- Price is local to the venue.
- A CEX last is not an AMM quote and not your fill.
- Companies can halt; a pool cannot halt unless pause() is in the code.
- During a halt, DEX prices can run while inventory is unwithdrawable.
- Arbitrage is not a law.

Next: volume is not truth.

lessons.title: Volume is not truth
lessons.content:
# Volume is not truth

**Volume** is a count of printed notional (or units) over a window. It can be economic trading. It can be **wash**: the same inventory walking back and forth to print a number. DEX wash is cheap because fees and gas can be low. A volume number is not a safety rating. Unique senders and **depth that actually fills** beat a banner.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to treat wash as theatre, and to refuse “high volume therefore honest pair” as a syllogism.

## Wash: same inventory, printed volume

On a book, wash can be two accounts (or one account with self-trade prevention off, or two affiliates) taking each other’s rest. The tape looks alive. Depth may still be a few hundred dollars at the inside. A $5,000 taker still walks off a cliff. The volume number will not catch you.

On a pool, wash is swapping back and forth, sometimes through a hop, sometimes with a fee-rebate token that refunds the fee. Cheap gas makes this a hobby. Unique **from** addresses on the explorer, looking at whether the same cluster dominates, is more informative than a 24h dollar figure on a listing site. You are not a prosecutor. You are a person who can walk away.

TABLE
Signal | Might mean | Does not mean
High 24h volume | Activity, or wash, or both | Safety
Tight spread, tiny size | A cartoon quote | You can take size
Many tiny swaps, same wallets | Wash / bot theatre | Organic flow
Unique senders + real depth | More interesting | Still not a blessing
Locked LP poster | A lock object, maybe | Volume is real
ENDTABLE

## Depth beats a volume number for a fill

If the question is “what happens if I take,” the answer is size at the inside and the next levels, or impact on the curve. Volume is a rear-view sum. Depth is the inventory still willing to meet you. Hidden orders mean even depth is incomplete on a book. On an AMM, reserves are visible; the hostile token in the pair is a different lesson.

Worked case. Pair advertises $40 million 24h volume. Inside bid size $180. Inside ask size $210. A notional of $8,000 will not fill like the banner. The volume was theatre, wash, or prints far from your intended price. You do not need a court filing to refuse the banner.

DIAGRAM
banner volume = sum of prints (maybe wash)
depth / reserves = inventory now
your fill depends on inventory now
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Do not use volume as a safety rating. This course will not send you to a “high-volume CST pair.” Unique senders and depth are literacy. They are still not a desk.
ENDNOTE

## Wash on AMMs

Self-trading against a pool still pays fees and still prints volume on chart sites. Volume without unique senders and without depth is a costume. CEX wash needs a venue that allows it or fails to stop it. You will not prosecute from a classroom. You will not treat a volume bar as demand.

## Crystal Stones volume on a screenshot

A CST volume spike on a random site is not homework and not a reason. If you ever read a pair for verification practice, you read reserves and holders, not a painted bar. Then you stop. No order.

## Unique senders, depth, and fees paid

On-chain you can look at how many distinct EOAs swapped and whether reserves moved. Painted volume often has few senders and little reserve change relative to the bar. Off-chain you cannot see senders. Treat CEX volume as a venue-reported integer, not as demand. Still no CST volume homework as a trade.

## Fee-paid volume versus painted prints

On an AMM, volume that paid pool fees and moved reserves is at least a trade-shaped event (still could be wash). Volume that did not move reserves is a costume. Off-chain, you often cannot tell. So you do not cite the bar. That is the whole skill.

## Say this out loud

- Wash is the same inventory printing volume.
- DEX wash is cheap when fees and gas are cheap.
- High volume with no depth is theatre.
- Unique senders plus depth beat a volume number.
- Volume is not a safety rating.
